name: Deep plane facelift
lead: A deep plane facelift is a facelift technique in which the surgeon dissects beneath the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and repositions the skin and SMAS together as a single composite flap. Descriptions of the extended version emphasize release of facial retaining ligaments so the flap can be moved to volumize the midface and the jawline [1][2].

It is used for midface, jawline and neck rejuvenation. General references describe it as reducing reliance on skin tension but as technically more demanding because the dissection lies close to facial nerve branches [3].

Published evidence is mainly surgeon case series, comparative studies and technique papers. One study with 75 patients used objective apparent-age assessment after facial rejuvenation surgery including deep-plane facelift [4].

paras: In the extended deep plane technique described by surgeons, four key retaining ligaments (zygomatic cutaneous, masseteric cutaneous, mandibular cutaneous and cervical) are released, and the composite flap is repositioned to volumize the midface and the gonial angle of the jaw [1]. Surgeons have published variants that extend the approach into the neck, such as a platysma hammock flap [5], vertical neck lifting [6], and a minimal-access hybrid with a vertical vector [7]. An endoscopic variant, the ponytail lift, was reported in a 22-year series of 600 cases [8]. Overview articles compare it with other facelift types [9].

One study of 75 patients (71 consecutive patients and four controls) objectively assessed change in apparent age after facial rejuvenation including deep-plane facelift and other cosmetic procedures [4]. A comparison of deep-plane and SMAS plication facelifts in the Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery examined how the techniques differ [10], and a later study looked at their effects on the midface [11]. Longevity of results was not quantified consistently in the sources reviewed; general references describe results from skin-only lifts as lasting around 5 to 10 years, with results varying by technique [3].

Facelift risks reported in general references include hematoma (the most common complication), nerve injury (the facial nerve being the most often injured motor nerve), skin necrosis (risk about twelve-fold higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion [3]. A meta-analysis of complication rates across SMAS facelift techniques noted that sub-SMAS techniques are considered to carry a higher complication profile, particularly for facial nerve injury, and that surgeons sometimes avoid sub-SMAS dissection for that reason [12]. A randomized, double-blind pilot study examined whether intravenous tranexamic acid affects bleeding during deep-plane facelift [13].
Deep-plane facelift combined with fascia lata graft has been reported as a static treatment for facial palsy in a preliminary report [14].

Human studies include the 75-patient apparent-age study [4], a randomized pilot study of tranexamic acid during deep-plane facelift [13], comparative studies with SMAS plication [10][11], and large technique series such as the 600-case ponytail lift report [8]. A registered study (NCT07910253, 4 participants, not yet recruiting) plans to examine deep-plane facelift as an adjunct to facial reanimation [15].

card.summary: A facelift that lifts skin and SMAS together as one unit with ligament release for the jawline, midface and neck; evidence is mostly surgeon series.
card.note: Major surgery near facial nerve branches; nerve injury and hematoma are reported risks.

quick.overview:
A deep plane facelift is a surgical facelift in which the surgeon lifts the skin and the underlying SMAS layer together as one unit after releasing ligaments that hold the face in place. It targets the midface, jawline and neck.

The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, plus a few comparative studies.
quick.mechanism: Releasing retaining ligaments lets the composite flap be repositioned to lift and volumize the midface and jaw, with less reliance on skin tension.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers) and scarring. Some surgeons consider sub-SMAS dissection to carry a higher facial nerve risk. It is major surgery.
